balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Charter Hall Group: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Charter Hall Group: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Charter Hall Group: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fum.title: Funds Under Management
fum.content:
FUM is the total value of the property, retail and diversified funds and mandates Charter Hall manages for investors; Property FUM is the subset in its core direct-property vehicles (excludes retail/diversified platform assets). Fee revenue is charged as a percentage of FUM, so FUM is the scale driver the whole earnings line runs off.

For Charter Hall Group: FUM fell from $87.4bn (FY2023) to $80.9bn (FY2024) as rising rates cut asset valuations and slowed inflows/transactions, then recovered to $94.3bn by FY2026 as rates eased -- a leading indicator of where fee income and Operating Earnings head next, roughly a year ahead of the earnings line.

What to watch:

  • FUM growth vs Operating Earnings growth (fee margin compression or expansion)
  • Property FUM as a share of total FUM (platform diversification)
  • Net inflows/transactions vs pure valuation movement -- the CSV shows the net level only

operatingVsStatutory.title: Operating Earnings vs statutory net income
operatingVsStatutory.content:
Operating Earnings is management's own earnings measure -- statutory profit adjusted to strip out property revaluations, gains/losses on derivatives and other non-cash or one-off items. It is the basis for distributions and the DCF's earnings base. Statutory net income is unadjusted IFRS profit, which swings with the property cycle because investment properties are marked to market every period.

For Charter Hall Group: FY2024 shows the gap at its widest -- a statutory net loss of -$222.1m (valuation write-downs as cap rates rose) against Operating Earnings of +$358.7m, positive and only modestly down on FY2023's $441.2m. Reading the statutory line alone would say the business lost money in FY2024; it did not -- fee income and performance fees stayed profitable throughout.

What to watch:

  • Direction of Operating Earnings through the cycle, independent of one period's cap-rate move
  • How large and how frequent the statutory/Operating gap is -- a persistently large gap means revaluations, not operations, are driving reported profit
  • Distributions are paid from Operating Earnings, not statutory profit, so this is the line that funds the payout

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Charter Hall Group: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Charter Hall Group: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Charter Hall Group: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Charter Hall Group: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Charter Hall Group: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Charter Hall Group: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
